name: Question 5
problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}-6y=-12{e}^{-2x}
$$

Consider the differential equation above, for which the corresponding complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-6x},$ where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants. Select the correct options below.$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{-2x}$ 
{{field-1}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{-2x}$ 
{{field-2}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The general solution of the differential equation is given by

$\,\,$
$y(x)=$ 
{{field-3}}
$+$
{{field-4}},

$\,$
where 
{{field-5}} are arbitrary constants.
worked_solution:
For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{c}(x)$ is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

- ${y}_{p}(x)$ is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{-2x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({e}^{-2x})^{′}=-2{e}^{-2x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =(-2{e}^{-2x})^{′}=4{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(4{e}^{-2x})+5(-2{e}^{-2x})-6({e}^{-2x})=-12{e}^{-2x}.\,\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{-2x}$ $\text{is}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

- For ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{-2x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =(x{e}^{-2x})^{′}={e}^{-2x}-2x{e}^{-2x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{-2x}-2x{e}^{-2x})^{′}=-4{e}^{-2x}+4x{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(-4{e}^{-2x}+4x{e}^{-2x})+5({e}^{-2x}-2x{e}^{-2x})-6(x{e}^{-2x})=-12{e}^{-2x}.\,\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{-2x}$ $\text{isn't}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-6x}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-6x}+{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $A\text{ and }B$ are arbitrary constants.

EXPLANATION

For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), where

  • yc(x) is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

  • yp(x) is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

  • For yp(x)=e−2x, we have y′(x)=(e−2x)′=−2e−2x,y″(x)=(−2e−2x)′=4e−2x. Substituting this into the equation, we have (4e−2x)+5(−2e−2x)−6(e−2x)=−12e−2x.✓ So, yp(x)=e−2x is a particular solution of the differential equation.

  • For yp(x)=xe−2x, we have y′(x)=(xe−2x)′=e−2x−2xe−2x,y″(x)=(e−2x−2xe−2x)′=−4e−2x+4xe−2x. Substituting this into the equation, we have (−4e−2x+4xe−2x)+5(e−2x−2xe−2x)−6(xe−2x)=−12e−2x.× So, yp(x)=xe−2x isn't a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is yc(x)=Aex+Be−6x. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x)=Aex+Be−6x+e−2x where A and B are arbitrary constants.
